title: A New Discovery at Göbekli Tepe Could Reshape Our Understanding of One of the Ancient World's Most Perplexing Sites
excerpt: The enigmatic Neolithic site of Göbekli Tepe in Turkey, home to some of the world’s earliest advanced megalithic construction and sophisticated symbolic art, continues to surprise archaeologists.
content:
The enigmatic Neolithic site of Göbekli Tepe in Turkey, home to some of the world’s earliest advanced megalithic construction and sophisticated symbolic art, continues to surprise archaeologists.

Since the discovery of megalithic features during excavations at the site led by archaeologist Klaus Schmidt in the 1990s, Göbekli Tepe has long been recognized as a ceremonial site, where its ancient builders might have gathered for ritual purposes under the site’s distinctive circles of T-shaped pillars.

At the time of its discovery, archaeologists had never found earlier examples of such sophisticated megalithic construction. Remarkably, Göbekli Tepe predated the appearance of monumental structures in Egypt, and even sites like Britain’s Stonehenge, by several thousands of years.

Yet despite the location’s impressiveness, its purpose seemed to be primarily a functional one: little evidence could be found that the ancient Neolithic site—built at a time that predates agriculture, and even the known use of pottery—had also been a dwelling place.

Now, new evidence suggests that parts of Göbekli Tepe may have indeed once been a habitation site, with the discovery of possible dwellings.

Possible Dwellings at the World’s Oldest Temple

Archaeologist Necmi Karul of Istanbul University and the Stone Hills Project recently revealed the results of geophysical surveys and new excavations being conducted at the ancient site, which have produced traces of several large structures that were long hidden beneath the ancient earth that still covers—and also protects—much of the site.

Although the purpose of these buildings remains unclear, evidence based on the internal arrangements within these ancient structures does seem to suggest they may have been living spaces, and even individual residences in some cases.

“Our first impression is that they [were] used as housing,” Karul said in a statement.

If confirmed, the discovery could add a new dimension to archaeologists’ understanding of the famous site, since it has long been presumed that its ancient inhabitants were primarily hunter-gatherers, who ranged throughout the region in search of sustenance during a time long before farming helped to facilitate the more sedentary lifestyle of later societies.

Göbekli Tepe: Reshaping Our Knowledge of the Ancient World

Although the discovery could change our understanding of Göbekli Tepe, it would align with past revelations about the site that have caused archaeologists to have to rethink things about the Neolithic world of ancient Anatolia, since it was also once presumed that hunter gatherers, due to their nomadic lifestyle, would have had little use for monumental architecture as far back as 11,000 years ago—and yet this is precisely what excavations at Göbekli Tepe revealed.

In a posting on social media, Turkey’s Minister of Culture and Tourism, Mehmet Nuri Ersoy, said that in addition to the discovery of the new possible habitation structures, ongoing work at the site continues to help ensure its conservation, and several of the structures at the site have been reinforced to help preserve them.

“We are also securing the monoliths against tremors using steel cables,” Ersoy said. “By simultaneously conducting excavation, restoration, and conservation work across various parts of Göbeklitepe, we are carrying this unique heritage into the future through a holistic approach.”
